paras: The lynching of Hardy Posey took place at Bessemer, Alabama, around midnight on April 23, 1888, when masked men took Posey, a Black man accused of attempting to rape a young white girl, from the town marshal and hanged him near the railroad depot. A placard on the body, signed "Bessemer's Best," declared that "our mothers, wives and daughters must and shall be protected." Telegraph reports that Black residents had risen to burn the town in revenge carried the story nationally, though next-day dispatches called the alarm exaggerated.

According to the Memphis Appeal, the accusation arose on Friday, April 20, at the home of a mechanic named McKinney just outside town, where his twelve-year-old adopted daughter said Posey seized her and threw her to the ground before her screams let her break away. The Appeal described Posey as 21 and a brother of Wesley Posey, whom troops had guarded from a mob after an alleged assault in 1883 and who later died in jail.

In the Appeal's account McKinney caught Posey in town and turned him over to the police, and on Saturday the girl picked him out from a line of Black men; the wire report said instead that he was caught on the morning of April 23. Because the lockup was well guarded, the marshal moved the prisoner to his own house on Monday night.

Soon after midnight, by the Charlotte Messenger's account, two hundred masked men came to the house and demanded Posey. The mob, the Appeal wrote, "made the marshal and the two policemen of the town go along with them and see the work well done." Posey was hanged from an oak near the depot, and the body hung until about nine the next morning, when the coroner cut it down.

On the evening of April 24 a messenger reached Birmingham saying about fifty armed Black men had gathered near Bessemer and a car of shingles had been burned. A dispatch sent after midnight said Black residents had "taken possession of the town," and Sheriff Truss called out the militia, until a telegram reported all quiet. The Memphis Appeal's correspondent wrote the next day that the scare rested on "pure conjecture," and that Posey was buried that day.

A later dispatch said Black laborers at the Sloss mines had offered to protect the town, and that two Black men tried to kill the girl's father, named as McKinney Foster, on April 26. No report of an inquest verdict or of any arrest of mob members appears in the coverage.

The AP dispatch ran on April 25 from Maine to California and Washington Territory, usually in two or three sentences that gave as much room to the threatened uprising as to the lynching. Headlines called Posey "a Fiend," "A Ravisher" and "A Negro Rapist," and the Rock Island Argus said Black residents "Object to Judge Lynch Tactics."

The Memphis Appeal printed the fullest account on its front page, treating the accusation as established and remarking that "Raping seems to run in the Posey family." The Savannah Morning News headed its report with the placard's signature, "Bessemer's Best." Northern summaries reduced the story to a line about the town being set afire.

Kansas weeklies in May printed both the report that Bessemer had been "in the hands of a negro mob" and the correction that the trouble "was much exaggerated," yet a September chronology still recorded the burning. Year-end lists of "Victims of Judge Lynch" entered Posey under April 23.

The girl was fifteen in the AP report, sixteen in the Indianapolis special, and twelve in the two detailed narratives, which also disagree on her name, Mamie or Alice McKinney. The Indianapolis special said Posey was taken "from the prison," but the Appeal and the Messenger agree it was the marshal's house. Most reports put the lynching on Monday night, but the Forrest City Times said Wednesday.

reader.title: Lynching of Hardy Posey
bases: A masked mob took Posey, a Black prisoner accused of attempted rape, from the town marshal and hanged him (A3, A8, A25).

Posey was hanged by a masked mob (two hundred men in A25) that took him from officers without any legal process (A8, A25), under a placard saying 'Our mothers, wives and daughters must and shall be protected' after an accusation of attempted rape (A3, A8).

The Memphis Appeal's Birmingham dispatch (A8), the AP report (A11), the Indianapolis Journal special (A3) and the Charlotte Messenger narrative (A25) agree on the hanging at Bessemer by a masked mob; the reported Black uprising afterward is contested (A3 vs A15, A22).

accounts.label: Memphis Appeal Birmingham correspondent
accounts.gist: Gives the girl's own account, the Saturday identification, the move to the marshal's house and the mob forcing the marshal and two policemen along; hanged from an oak in the center of town.

accounts.label: AP wire report
accounts.gist: Posey caught on the morning of April 23 and identified, hanged near the depot with a placard; the town said to be surrounded by armed negroes threatening to burn it.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal special
accounts.gist: Posey taken 'from the prison' by masked men; a 12:50 a.m. report said Black residents had taken possession of Bessemer and begun to burn it, and armed men left Birmingham.

accounts.label: Charlotte Messenger narrative
accounts.gist: Two hundred quiet masked white men took Posey from the marshal's residence and hanged him fifty feet from the depot; placard signed 'Bessemer's Best Citizens'; coroner cut him down at 9 a.m.

accounts.label: Next-day Birmingham dispatches
accounts.gist: Fifty armed Black men and a burned shingle car were reported, but quiet returned; the Memphis Appeal said nothing happened to justify the scare.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal treated the accusation as fact, printed the girl's account and wrote that 'Raping seems to run in the Posey family.'
Most papers ran the two-sentence AP brief under headlines such as 'The Lynching of a Fiend Causes an Uprising of Negroes', 'A Ravisher Lynched' and 'A Negro Rapist Lynched'.
Northern news summaries reduced the event to Black residents setting fire to the town in revenge; the Rock Island Argus headed it 'They Object to Judge Lynch Tactics'.
